subject: clockworkDog
reasoning:
I'm planning out a TypeScript module for building a clockwork dog with the SDK, designing it as a realistic quadruped around dog-sized proportions with a brass body, visible gears, a wind-up key, rivets, a glass eye, jointed legs, and a spring-coil tail.

I'm reviewing the key builder APIs available—joints, chains, sweeps, parts, surfaces, and limb helpers—and thinking through how to achieve a brassy look using plain colors or a grain paint for sheen, then roughing out the body's coordinate scale with hips around 0.55m high and legs about 0.3m long to the floor.

Now I'm sketching the skeleton structure: placing the hips joint as root, building a spine chain from hips to chest using a catmull path, then a neck chain extending up to the head base, working out how chain names and parent relationships map onto spine and neck segments.

Then I'm figuring out the head joint position and aim direction coming off the neck's final joint, followed by adding a jaw joint parented to the head with a local offset for the aim target, and considering whether to build the skull shape as a lathe or sweep geometry.

I'm working out the frustumBox helper to build a blocky head shape, using local offsets along the head joint's forward/up axes to define the box's start and end widths and heights.

I realize the "words" form (forward/up/right) refers to fixed model-space directions rather than bone-relative orientation, so I can use consistent offsets for the snout, jaw, and other head parts without worrying about each bone's own rotation. Now I'm adding glass eye spheres positioned via head.local with right/forward offsets.

Thinking through brass ring studs around each eye using the ring helper with small embedded sphere sticks, then moving to flat triangular ear fins extruded as plates oriented in the forward-up plane so they sit sideways when viewed from the front.

Now I'm working out the four legs using the limb helper, defining front legs as simple two-segment limbs with forward knee bends, and hind legs as digitigrade three-segment limbs with hip-knee-hock joints and alternating bend directions to get a proper dog-like stance.

I'm checking that shoulder and hip joint positions, leg segment lengths, and target foot positions actually reach the ground without overstretching -- adjusting shoulder height and segment lengths so the front paws land correctly on the floor plane.

Now I'm scaling the whole dog's proportions down to feel toy-sized rather than full dog height, recalculating leg lengths and spine endpoints at hips and chest. I'm planning the body as a sweep along a spine curve from hips to chest with a varying radius function to give it a barrel shape, thicker at the chest.

For the surface treatment, I'm deciding between stripes, patches, or scales to give the clockwork body a riveted brass-plate look, leaning toward scales for the outlined, paneled effect. I'm picking out a brass/copper/iron color palette and considering adding a clockwork key detail on the flank as a surface attachment.

For the key, I'm finding a surface point on the body and sticking a flat cylinder along the normal so it protrudes sideways like a gear-shaped winding key. I'm also working out how to scatter small rivet spheres directly onto the body surface rather than along the spine, since surface placement is needed for them to sit properly embedded.

Now I'm considering a simpler approach: sweeping a closed loop around the body's cross-section to create a brass trim ring, using a surface loop cut by a plane facing the Z-axis at a chosen point along the spine.

For the head, I'm sketching out proportions for skull, snout, and jaw as frustum boxes positioned relative to the head joint, then adding a jaw hinge joint and a small iron sphere for the nose tip at the snout's end.

Now I'm working out how to place triangular ear plates on either side of the head using extrude geometry, figuring out the local axis conventions for left/right placement and settling on signed offsets to position each ear symmetrically.

For the tail, I'm sketching a chain of segments curving from the hips backward and upward like a coiled clockwork spring, tapering the sweep radius along its length and planning brass-colored banding to give it a segmented, mechanical look.

For decoration, I'm considering adding visible clock-gear details on the flank and a winding-key accent on top of the hips, built as a small lathe shape anchored to a surface hit point with its axis aligned to the body's normal there.

For the gears themselves, I'm figuring out how to fake a toothed disc using a cylinder for the body and a ring of small cube teeth arranged around it, oriented outward along the surface normal.

I'm working through how to set up the leg chains attached to the body's torso surface, figuring out the right parent joints and naming conventions for front and hind legs so each chain's tip lands correctly at the paw.

Now I'm designing the paw geometry itself, positioning a small frustum shape at each foot joint to form the pad, and checking the orientation and height so it sits just above the floor rather than sinking into it.

For the legs, I'm planning a sweep along each limb chain with tapering radius—thicker near the hip/shoulder, narrowing toward the ankle—and adding small sphere joints at the knee/elbow to visually mark the bend, figuring out how to anchor those spheres to the correct joint frame.

Now I'm working out the spine and neck geometry, defining the chest point and a spine path with catmull-rom segments running from the lower back up to the chest, then figuring out how the neck should continue that curve up toward the head joint.

I need to give the neck chain a proper tip joint so the head has something to parent to—adding a "neckTip" name gives the head joint a clear attachment point with its own aim direction. For the hips, I'm debating whether to make it the root joint or reuse the spine1 position; I'll settle on a separate hips root positioned slightly behind the spine start, aiming forward, so the spine chain can parent cleanly off it without duplicate overlapping joints.

I'll just accept the tiny coincident-joint offset and move on rather than overthink the exact geometry. For limb attachments, hind legs parent to hips and front legs parent to the chest tip, with shoulder and hip points positioned slightly outboard, and the leg chains will need plane-bend hints for proper IK bending direction.

Let me work through the lengths and distances for front and hind limbs so the chain segments reach their paw targets without being too short, adjusting bend hints so knees point forward and hocks point backward. For materials, I'll use a brass-toned scale texture on the body and a stripe pattern along the tail axis.

Now I'm figuring out the import structure, keeping everything from a single module, and placing amber glass eye spheres using local bone coordinates scaled to the skull's width. I'm also setting up a small ring of brass stud details around each eye socket.

Working through how to orient the eye ring so it aims outward along the gaze direction rather than straight up — defining a line between the eye center and a point offset outward along the head's local axis, then using that line as the frame for the ring of stick elements.

I'm also figuring out placement for other features: using nearest-point lookups on the body mesh to find flank positions for the gear and rivet band, and the top of the head for the key's lathe shape, picking axis directions that match each surface's normal.

Now I'm sketching the skull and snout using frustumBox shapes attached to the head bone, then working out the jaw joint position and its own frustum geometry beneath the snout.

I still need to figure out the jaw's aim direction and hinge rotation—using b.joint to set up the pivot and b.pose with an axis/degree rotation to give it a slight open-mouth tilt, deciding whether to pose before or after building the jaw's geometry since handles stay valid either way.

For the body details, I'm planning out teeth as small upward-pointing spikes along the jaw, leather ear shapes built from outline points, and the torso/leg/tail geometry using swept chains with tapering radii, plus knee and hock spheres at the joints. The tail gets a catmull-rom curve with torus "spring" segments oriented via frame orientation along the tangent.

For decoration, I'm adding brass rivets scattered around a surface loop at the torso's midsection, plus two meshing clockwork gears (with teeth as small boxes in a ring) stuck onto the flank, and a winding key near the top of the hips. I'm also settling on a brass/copper/iron/leather color palette for the body, head, legs, and jaw, and double-checking that every helper variable I reference is actually used so the code stays clean.

Now I'm working out the skeleton hierarchy in detail — hips, spine chain, neck, head, and jaw joints, followed by front and hind leg limb chains using inverse-kinematic bends, and tail chain — making sure joint names match the required naming pattern and chains get the right number of names relative to their path spans so tips resolve correctly without unintended zero-length bones.
